class="prose" id="body"><section class="art-section" data-reveal="" style="--reveal-delay:.1s" id="lessons-from-building-claude-code-how-we-use-skills-s0"><p>Skills have become one of the most used extension points in Claude Code. They’re flexible, easy to make, and easy to distribute.</p>
<p>But this flexibility also makes it hard to know what works best. What type of skills are worth making? How do you structure a skill? When do you share them with others?</p>
<p>We&#x27;ve been using skills in Claude Code extensively at Anthropic with hundreds of them in active use. These are the lessons we&#x27;ve learned about using skills to accelerate our development.</p>
</section><section class="art-section" data-reveal="" style="--reveal-delay:.1s" id="lessons-from-building-claude-code-how-we-use-skills-s1"><h2 id="what-are-skills">WHAT ARE SKILLS?</h2>
<p>Skills are folders of instructions, scripts, and resources that agents can discover and use to do things more accurately and efficiently. This blog post assumes familiarity with skills basics; if you’re new, start with our <a href="https://anthropic.skilljar.com/introduction-to-agent-skills">Introduction to agent skills course on Skilljar</a>.</p>
<p>A common misconception we hear about skills is that they are “just markdown files.” They’re actually folders that can include scripts, assets, data, etc. that the agent can discover, explore and manipulate.</p>
<p>In Claude Code, skills also have a <a href="https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills#frontmatter-reference">wide variety of configuration options</a> including registering dynamic hooks.</p>
<p>We’ve found that some of the most effective skills in Claude Code use these configuration options and folder structure effectively.</p>
</section><section class="art-section" data-reveal="" style="--reveal-delay:.1s" id="lessons-from-building-claude-code-how-we-use-skills-s2"><h2 id="types-of-skills">TYPES OF SKILLS</h2>
<p>After cataloging all of our internal skills at Anthropic, we noticed they cluster into nine categories. The best skills fit cleanly into one; the ones that try to do too much straddle several and confuse the agent. This isn&#x27;t a definitive list, but it is a useful framework for identifying gaps in your own skills library.</p>
<figure class="art-fig"><img class="fg" src="/media/8c0b43b7a1f0aefab9af8990f3d69eb961d4c5eef12c1e72584828787e57cb5f.png" alt="A three-by-three grid of skill categories with example skill names: Library and API Reference, Product Verification, Data and Analysis, Business Automation, Scaffolding and Templates, Code Quality and Review, CI/CD and Deployment, Incident Runbooks, Infrastructure Ops." loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="2048" height="1148" style="display:block;width:100%;aspect-ratio:2048 / 1148"/><figcaption class="cap"><b>FIG A</b><span>The Claude Code team categorized our internal skills and found that they could be bucketed into nine distinct categories.</span></figcaption></figure>
<h3 id="1-library-and-api-reference">1. Library and API reference</h3>
<p>These are skills that explain how to correctly use a library, CLI, or SDKs. They could be both for internal libraries or common libraries that Claude Code sometimes struggles to handle. These skills often included a folder of reference code snippets and a list of gotchas for Claude to avoid when writing a script.</p>
<p>Examples include:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>billing-lib</code> — your internal billing library: edge cases, footguns, etc.</li>
<li><code>internal-platform-cli</code> — every subcommand of your internal CLI wrapper with examples on when to use them.</li>
<li><code>sandbox-proxy</code> — configuring your org&#x27;s egress gateway for dev work: which hosts are reachable, how to debug &quot;connection refused&quot; errors, how to add an allowlist entry.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="2-product-verification">2. Product verification</h3>
<p>These are skills that describe how to test or verify that your code is working. They are often paired with playwright, tmux, or other external tools for verification.</p>
<p>Verification skills have had the most measurable impact on Claude’s output quality internally. It can be worth having an engineer spend a week just making your verification skills excellent.</p>
<p>Consider techniques like having Claude record a video of its output so you can see exactly what it tested, or enforcing programmatic assertions on state at each step. These are often done by including a variety of scripts in the skill.</p>
<p>Examples include:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>signup-flow-driver</code> — runs through signup → email verify → onboarding in a headless browser, with hooks for asserting state at each step</li>
<li><code>checkout-verifier</code> — drives the checkout UI with Stripe test cards, verifies the invoice actually lands in the right state</li>
<li><code>tmux-cli-driver</code> — for interactive CLI testing where the thing you&#x27;re verifying needs a TTY</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="3-data-fetching-and-analysis">3. Data fetching and analysis</h3>
<p>These are skills that connect to your data and monitoring stacks. These skills might include libraries to fetch your data with credentials, specific dashboard ids, etc., as well as instructions on common workflows or ways to get data.</p>
<p>Examples include:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>funnel-query</code> — &quot;which events do I join to see signup → activation → paid&quot; plus the table that actually has the canonical user_id</li>
<li><code>cohort-compare</code> — compare two cohorts&#x27; retention or conversion, flag statistically significant deltas, link to the segment definitions</li>
<li><code>grafana</code> — datasource UIDs, cluster names, problem → dashboard lookup table</li>
<li><code>datadog</code> — field reference (@request_id vs trace_id), service list, metric prefix conventions</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="4-business-process-and-team-automation">4. Business process and team automation</h3>
<p>These are skills that automate repetitive workflows into one command. These skills are usually fairly simple instructions but might have more complicated dependencies on other skills or MCPs. For these skills, saving previous results in log files can help the model stay consistent and reflect on previous executions of the workflow.</p>
<p>Examples include:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>standup-post</code> — aggregates your ticket tracker, GitHub activity, and prior Slack → formatted standup, delta-only</li>
<li><code>create-&lt;ticket-system&gt;-ticket</code> — enforces schema (valid enum values, required fields) plus post-creation workflow (ping reviewer, link in Slack)</li>
<li><code>weekly-recap</code> — merged PRs + closed tickets + deploys → formatted recap post</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="5-code-scaffolding-and-templates">5. Code scaffolding and templates</h3>
<p>These are skills that generate framework boilerplates for a specific function in a codebase. You might combine these skills with scripts that can be composed. They are especially useful when your scaffolding has natural language requirements that can’t be purely covered by code.</p>
<p>Examples include:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>new-&lt;framework&gt;-workflow</code> — scaffolds a new service/workflow/handler with your annotations</li>
<li><code>new-migration</code> — your migration file template plus common gotchas</li>
<li><code>create-app</code> — new internal app with your auth, logging, and deploy config pre-wired</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="6-code-quality-and-review">6. Code quality and review</h3>
<p>These are skills that enforce code quality inside of your org and help review code. These can include deterministic scripts or tools for maximum robustness. You may want to run these skills automatically as part of hooks or inside of a GitHub Action.</p>
<ul>
<li><code>adversarial-review</code> — spawns a fresh-eyes subagent to critique, implements fixes, iterates until findings degrade to nitpicks</li>
<li><code>code-style</code> — enforces code style, especially styles that Claude does not do well by default.</li>
<li><code>testing-practices</code> — instructions on how to write tests and what to test.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="7-cicd-and-deployment">7. CI/CD and deployment</h3>
<p>These are skills that help you fetch, push, and deploy code inside of your codebase. These skills may reference other skills to collect data.</p>
<p>Examples include:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>babysit-pr</code> — monitors a PR → retries flaky CI → resolves merge conflicts → enables auto-merge</li>
<li><code>deploy-&lt;service&gt;</code> — build → smoke test → gradual traffic rollout with error-rate comparison → auto-rollback on regression</li>
<li><code>cherry-pick-prod</code> — isolated worktree → cherry-pick → conflict resolution → PR with template</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="8-runbooks">8. Runbooks</h3>
<p>These are skills that take a symptom (such as a Slack thread, alert, or error signature), walk through a multi-tool investigation, and produce a structured report.</p>
<p>Examples include:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>&lt;service&gt;-debugging</code> — maps symptoms → tools → query patterns for your highest-traffic services</li>
<li><code>oncall-runner</code> — fetches the alert → checks the usual suspects → formats a finding</li>
<li><code>log-correlator</code> — given a request ID, pulls matching logs from every system that might have touched it</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="9-infrastructure-operations">9. Infrastructure operations</h3>
<p>These are skills that perform routine maintenance and operational procedures, some of which involve destructive actions that benefit from guardrails. These make it easier for engineers to follow best practices in critical operations.</p>
<p>Examples include:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>&lt;resource&gt;-orphans</code> — finds orphaned pods/volumes → posts to Slack → soak period → user confirms → cascading cleanup</li>
<li><code>dependency-management</code> — your org&#x27;s dependency approval workflow</li>
<li><code>cost-investigation</code> — &quot;why did our storage/egress bill spike&quot; with the specific buckets and query patterns</li>
</ul>
</section><section class="art-section" data-reveal="" style="--reveal-delay:.1s" id="lessons-from-building-claude-code-how-we-use-skills-s3"><h2 id="tips-for-making-skills">TIPS FOR MAKING SKILLS</h2>
<p>Once you&#x27;ve decided on the skill to make, how do you write it? These are some of the Claude Code team’s best practices, tips, and tricks for making skills.</p>
<h3 id="dont-state-the-obvious">Don’t state the obvious</h3>
<p>Claude already knows how to code and can read your codebase. A skill that restates what Claude would do by default adds context without adding value. If you’re publishing a skill that is primarily about knowledge, focus on information that pushes Claude out of its normal way of thinking.</p>
<p>The <a href="https://github.com/anthropics/skills/blob/main/skills/frontend-design/SKILL.md">frontend design skill</a> is a great example; it was built by an engineer at Anthropic by iterating with customers on improving Claude’s design taste, avoiding classic patterns like the Inter font and purple gradients.</p>
<h3 id="build-a-gotchas-section">Build a gotchas section</h3>
<figure class="art-fig"><img class="fg" src="/media/16acf64a5f80810ad01275e7a7de64b689ff947b145ee1b188f328e614cdfe98.png" alt="The same Billing Lib skill file on day 1, week 2 and month 3. A Gotchas section appears and grows from one line (proration rounds down) to four." loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="820" height="360" style="display:block;width:100%;aspect-ratio:820 / 360"/></figure>
<p>The highest-signal content in any skill is the Gotchas section. These sections should be built up from common failure points that Claude runs into when using your skill. Ideally, you will update your skill over time to capture these gotchas.</p>
<p>For example:</p>
<ul>
<li>&quot;The <code>subscriptions</code> table is append-only. The row you want is the one with the highest version, not the most recent <code>created_at</code>.&quot;</li>
<li>&quot;This field is called <code>@request_id</code> in the API gateway and <code>trace_id</code> in the billing service. They&#x27;re the same value.&quot;</li>
<li>&quot;Staging returns 200 even when the Stripe webhook didn&#x27;t actually process. Check <code>payment_events</code> for the real state.&quot;</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="use-the-file-system-and-progressive-disclosure">Use the file system and progressive disclosure</h3>
<figure class="art-fig"><img class="fg" src="/media/d70d147c4c600c297d350ebd7a76f110c879ca670f9e40adb83b05882f71dd8c.png" alt="A queue-debugging skill folder where SKILL.md is the hub and stuck-jobs.md, dead-letters.md, retry-storms.md and consumer-lag.md are spokes. SKILL.md holds a symptom-to-file table telling Claude which file to read." loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="2048" height="930" style="display:block;width:100%;aspect-ratio:2048 / 930"/><figcaption class="cap"><b>FIG B</b><span>The SKILL.md file points to several other files Claude can reference for specific situations. For example, if a job is pending, it should reference stuck-jobs.md.</span></figcaption></figure>
<p>Like we said earlier, a skill is a folder, not just a markdown file. You should think of the entire file system as a form of context engineering and progressive disclosure. Tell Claude what files are in your skill, and it will read them at appropriate times.</p>
<p>The simplest form of progressive disclosure is to point to other markdown files for Claude to use. For example, you may split detailed function signatures and usage examples into <code>references/api.md</code>.</p>
<p>Another example: if your end output is a markdown file, you might include a template file for it in <code>assets/</code> to copy and use.</p>
<p>You can have folders of references, scripts, examples, etc., which help Claude work more effectively.</p>
<h3 id="avoid-railroading-claude">Avoid railroading Claude</h3>
<p>Claude will generally try to stick to your instructions, and because skills are so reusable you’ll want to be careful of being too specific in your instructions. Give Claude the information it needs, but give it the flexibility to adapt to the situation.</p>
<p>For example:</p>
<figure class="art-fig"><img class="fg" src="/media/f634d39724ba5a2785fa6a8aa5614a1e4654c1d278a2d73b0e3b7ce0a74d84c4.png" alt="Two versions of cherry-pick instructions. Too prescriptive: six numbered steps spelling out each git command. Better: “Cherry-pick the commit onto a clean branch. Resolve conflicts preserving intent. If it can’t land cleanly, explain why.”" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1440" height="660" style="display:block;width:100%;aspect-ratio:1440 / 660"/><figcaption class="cap"><b>FIG C</b><span>State the goal and the constraints, not every step.</span></figcaption></figure>
<h3 id="think-through-the-setup">Think through the setup</h3>
<figure class="art-fig"><img class="fg" src="/media/c24d1f6d68756396e649a2a1ee89dcde197dad5675e9b75cf17099064345486e.png" alt="A standup-post SKILL.md whose “Your config” section runs a shell command reading config.json and echoing NOT_CONFIGURED if it is missing; the instructions tell Claude to ask for the Slack channel and a sample standup when unconfigured, then save the answers." loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1404" height="818" style="display:block;width:100%;aspect-ratio:1404 / 818"/><figcaption class="cap"><b>FIG D</b><span>The skill above is written to prompt the user if the Slack channel is not included in the configuration.</span></figcaption></figure>
<p>Some skills may need to be set up with context from the user. For example, if you are making a skill that posts your standup to Slack, you may want Claude to ask which Slack channel to post it in.</p>
<p>A good pattern to do this is to store this setup information in a config.json file in the skill directory like the above example. If the config is not set up, the agent can then ask the user for information.</p>
<p>If you want the agent to present structured, multiple choice questions you can instruct Claude to use the AskUserQuestion tool.</p>
<h3 id="write-descriptions-for-the-model-not-for-humans">Write descriptions for the model, not for humans</h3>
<p>When Claude Code starts a session, it builds a listing of every available skill with its description. This listing is what Claude scans to decide &quot;is there a skill for this request?&quot; Which means the description field is not a summary, it&#x27;s a description of when to trigger this skill.</p>
<figure class="art-fig"><img class="fg" src="/media/1debbf1fd04f39bcfeb62bcb458574268414bd0f519c4390d708bbac8f1b724e.png" alt="Two SKILL.md descriptions for babysit-pr. Left: “A comprehensive tool for monitoring pull request status across the development lifecycle.” Right: “Monitors a PR until it merges. Trigger on ‘babysit’, ‘watch CI’, ‘make sure this lands’.”" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1640" height="460" style="display:block;width:100%;aspect-ratio:1640 / 460"/><figcaption class="cap"><b>FIG E</b><span>It’s helpful to include triggers for the skill, like “babysit,” in its description.</span></figcaption></figure>
<h3 id="help-claude-remember">Help Claude remember</h3>
<figure class="art-fig"><img class="fg" src="/media/829d6345a17c88a8eb51d616918194402492d1afaba783b00e8b5fdf06b89edf.png" alt="A ~/.claude/standups.log file with dated entries for three consecutive days; the onboarding redesign thread is highlighted across all of them." loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1440" height="660" style="display:block;width:100%;aspect-ratio:1440 / 660"/><figcaption class="cap"><b>FIG F</b><span>This text log file helps Claude remember past events like reviewing Sarah’s auth PR.</span></figcaption></figure>
<p>Some skills can include a form of memory by storing data within them. You could store data in anything as simple as an append only text log file or JSON files, or as complicated as a SQLite database.</p>
<p>For example, a <code>standup-post</code> skill might keep a standups.log with every post it&#x27;s written, which means the next time you run it, Claude reads its own history and can tell what&#x27;s changed since yesterday.</p>
<p>You can use the env variable <code>${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}</code> to get a stable directory where you can store data, read more persisting data in skills here: <a href="https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins-reference#persistent-data-directory">https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins-reference#persistent-data-directory</a>.</p>
<h3 id="store-scripts-and-generate-code">Store scripts and generate code</h3>
<p>One of the most powerful tools you can give Claude is code. Giving Claude scripts and libraries lets Claude spend its turns on composition, deciding what to do next rather than reconstructing boilerplate.</p>
<p>For example, in your <code>data-science</code> skill you might have a library of functions to fetch data from your event source. In order for Claude to do complex analysis, you could give it a set of helper functions like this:</p>
<figure class="art-fig"><img class="fg" src="/media/9306b89148d50e676d639a58b675a7461b8df96079f41db272558651be023f5f.png" alt="lib/signups.py with three helper functions, fetch, by_referrer and by_landing_page, whose docstrings record data gotchas such as user_id being null until after signup." loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1440" height="760" style="display:block;width:100%;aspect-ratio:1440 / 760"/><figcaption class="cap"><b>FIG G</b><span>Give Claude a small library of helpers with the gotchas written into the docstrings.</span></figcaption></figure>
<p>Claude can then generate scripts on the fly to compose this functionality to do more advanced analysis for prompts like “What happened on Tuesday?”</p>
<figure class="art-fig"><img class="fg" src="/media/58c7ef840b2a94594f712995ad204a05360a28f0a02c74931a5c238c11426fa5.png" alt="investigate.py, generated by Claude, importing those helpers to compare Monday and Tuesday signups by referrer and landing page and concluding that something broke on the homepage on Tuesday." loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1440" height="540" style="display:block;width:100%;aspect-ratio:1440 / 540"/><figcaption class="cap"><b>FIG H</b><span>Claude composes the helpers into a one-off script for the question at hand.</span></figcaption></figure>
<h3 id="use-on-demand-hooks">Use on-demand hooks</h3>
<p>Skills can include hooks that are only activated when the skill is called, and that only last for the duration of the session. Use this for more opinionated hooks that you don’t want to run all the time, but are extremely useful sometimes.</p>
<p>For example:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong><code>/careful</code></strong> — blocks rm -rf, DROP TABLE, force-push, kubectl delete via PreToolUse matcher on Bash. You only want this when you know you&#x27;re touching prod — having it always on would drive you insane.</li>
<li><strong><code>/freeze</code></strong> — blocks any Edit/Write that&#x27;s not in a specific directory. Useful during debugging: &quot;I want to add logs but I keep accidentally &#x27;fixing&#x27; unrelated code.&quot;</li>
</ul>
</section><section class="art-section" data-reveal="" style="--reveal-delay:.1s" id="lessons-from-building-claude-code-how-we-use-skills-s4"><h2 id="distributing-skills">DISTRIBUTING SKILLS</h2>
<p>One of the biggest benefits of skills is that you can share them with the rest of your team.</p>
<p>There are two ways you might want to share skills with others:</p>
<ul>
<li>check your skills into your repo (under <code>./.claude/skills</code>)</li>
<li>make a <strong>plugin</strong> and have a Claude Code Plugin marketplace where users can upload and install plugins (read more on the <a href="https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-marketplaces">documentation</a> here)</li>
</ul>
<p>For smaller teams working across relatively few repos, checking your skills into repos works well. But every skill that is checked in also adds a little bit to the context of the model. As you scale, an internal plugin marketplace allows you to distribute skills and let your team decide which ones to install, as well as include a setup flow.</p>
</section><section class="art-section" data-reveal="" style="--reveal-delay:.1s" id="lessons-from-building-claude-code-how-we-use-skills-s5"><h2 id="managing-a-skills-marketplace">MANAGING A SKILLS MARKETPLACE</h2>
<p>How do you decide which skills go in a marketplace? How do people submit them?</p>
<p>At Anthropic, we don&#x27;t have a centralized team that decides; instead we try to find the most useful skills organically. If someone has a skill that they want people to try out, they can upload it to a sandbox folder in GitHub and point people to it in Slack or other forums.</p>
<p>Once a skill has gotten traction (which is up to the skill owner to decide), they can put in a PR to move it into the marketplace.</p>
</section><section class="art-section" data-reveal="" style="--reveal-delay:.1s" id="lessons-from-building-claude-code-how-we-use-skills-s6"><h2 id="composing-skills">COMPOSING SKILLS</h2>
<p>You may want to have skills that depend on each other. For example, you may have a file upload skill that uploads a file, and a CSV generation skill that makes a CSV and uploads it. This sort of dependency management is not natively built into marketplaces or skills yet, but you can just reference other skills by name, and the model will invoke them if they are installed.</p>
</section><section class="art-section" data-reveal="" style="--reveal-delay:.1s" id="lessons-from-building-claude-code-how-we-use-skills-s7"><h2 id="measuring-skills">MEASURING SKILLS</h2>
<p>To understand how a skill is doing, we use a PreToolUse hook that lets us log skill usage within the company (<a href="https://gist.github.com/ThariqS/24defad423d701746e23dc19aace4de5">example code here</a>). This means we can find skills that are popular or are undertriggering compared to our expectations.</p>
</section><section class="art-section" data-reveal="" style="--reveal-delay:.1s" id="lessons-from-building-claude-code-how-we-use-skills-s8"><h2 id="get-started">GET STARTED</h2>
<p>Skills best practices are still evolving. Most of our best skills began as a few lines and a single gotcha, then got better because people kept adding to them as Claude hit new edge cases.</p>
<p>The best way to understand skills is to get started, experiment, and see what works for you.</p>
<ul>
<li>Check out <a href="https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills">our skills documentation</a></li>
<li><a href="https://github.com/anthropics/skills">Find example skills to customize</a></li>
</ul>
<p><em>This article was written by Thariq Shihipar, a member of technical staff at Anthropic, working on Claude Code.</em></p></section></div></div><div class="more-sec"><div class="rel-lbl">Related They’re flexible, easy to make, and easy to distribute.\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"But this flexibility also makes it hard to know what works best. What type of skills are worth making? How do you structure a skill? When do you share them with others?\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"We've been using skills in Claude Code extensively at Anthropic with hundreds of them in active use. These are the lessons we've learned about using skills to accelerate our development.\"}],\"\\n\"]}],[\"$\",\"section\",null,{\"className\":\"art-section\",\"data-reveal\":\"\",\"style\":\"$2b:0:props:style\",\"id\":\"lessons-from-building-claude-code-how-we-use-skills-s1\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"h2\",null,{\"id\":\"what-are-skills\",\"children\":[\"WHAT ARE SKILLS?\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":[\"Skills are folders of instructions, scripts, and resources that agents can discover and use to do things more accurately and efficiently. This blog post assumes familiarity with skills basics; if you’re new, start with our \",[\"$\",\"a\",null,{\"href\":\"https://anthropic.skilljar.com/introduction-to-agent-skills\",\"children\":\"Introduction to agent skills course on Skilljar\"}],\".\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"A common misconception we hear about skills is that they are “just markdown files.” They’re actually folders that can include scripts, assets, data, etc. that the agent can discover, explore and manipulate.\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":[\"In Claude Code, skills also have a \",[\"$\",\"a\",null,{\"href\":\"https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills#frontmatter-reference\",\"children\":\"wide variety of configuration options\"}],\" including registering dynamic hooks.\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"We’ve found that some of the most effective skills in Claude Code use these configuration options and folder structure effectively.\"}],\"\\n\"]}],[\"$\",\"section\",null,{\"className\":\"art-section\",\"data-reveal\":\"\",\"style\":\"$2b:0:props:style\",\"id\":\"lessons-from-building-claude-code-how-we-use-skills-s2\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"h2\",null,{\"id\":\"types-of-skills\",\"children\":[\"TYPES OF SKILLS\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"After cataloging all of our internal skills at Anthropic, we noticed they cluster into nine categories. The best skills fit cleanly into one; the ones that try to do too much straddle several and confuse the agent. This isn't a definitive list, but it is a useful framework for identifying gaps in your own skills library.\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"figure\",null,{\"className\":\"art-fig\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"img\",null,{\"className\":\"fg\",\"src\":\"/media/8c0b43b7a1f0aefab9af8990f3d69eb961d4c5eef12c1e72584828787e57cb5f.png\",\"alt\":\"A three-by-three grid of skill categories with example skill names: Library and API Reference, Product Verification, Data and Analysis, Business Automation, Scaffolding and Templates, Code Quality and Review, CI/CD and Deployment, Incident Runbooks, Infrastructure Ops.\",\"loading\":\"lazy\",\"decoding\":\"async\",\"width\":2048,\"height\":1148,\"style\":{\"display\":\"block\",\"width\":\"100%\",\"aspectRatio\":\"2048 / 1148\"}}],[\"$\",\"figcaption\",null,{\"className\":\"cap\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"b\",null,{\"children\":\"FIG A\"}],\"$undefined\",[\"$\",\"span\",null,{\"children\":\"The Claude Code team categorized our internal skills and found that they could be bucketed into nine distinct categories.\"}]]}]]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"1-library-and-api-reference\",\"children\":\"1. Library and API reference\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"These are skills that explain how to correctly use a library, CLI, or SDKs. They could be both for internal libraries or common libraries that Claude Code sometimes struggles to handle. These skills often included a folder of reference code snippets and a list of gotchas for Claude to avoid when writing a script.\"}],\"\\n\",\"$L2d\",\"\\n\",\"$L2e\",\"\\n\",\"$L2f\",\"\\n\",\"$L30\",\"\\n\",\"$L31\",\"\\n\",\"$L32\",\"\\n\",\"$L33\",\"\\n\",\"$L34\",\"\\n\",\"$L35\",\"\\n\",\"$L36\",\"\\n\",\"$L37\",\"\\n\",\"$L38\",\"\\n\",\"$L39\",\"\\n\",\"$L3a\",\"\\n\",\"$L3b\",\"\\n\",\"$L3c\",\"\\n\",\"$L3d\",\"\\n\",\"$L3e\",\"\\n\",\"$L3f\",\"\\n\",\"$L40\",\"\\n\",\"$L41\",\"\\n\",\"$L42\",\"\\n\",\"$L43\",\"\\n\",\"$L44\",\"\\n\",\"$L45\",\"\\n\",\"$L46\",\"\\n\",\"$L47\",\"\\n\",\"$L48\",\"\\n\",\"$L49\",\"\\n\",\"$L4a\",\"\\n\",\"$L4b\",\"\\n\",\"$L4c\",\"\\n\",\"$L4d\",\"\\n\",\"$L4e\",\"\\n\",\"$L4f\",\"\\n\"]}],\"$L50\",\"$L51\",\"$L52\",\"$L53\",\"$L54\",\"$L55\"]\n2d:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Examples include:\"}]\n2e:[\"$\",\"ul\",null,{\"children\":[\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"billing-lib\"}],\" — your internal billing library: edge cases, footguns, etc.\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"internal-platform-cli\"}],\" — every subcommand of your internal CLI wrapper with examples on when to use them.\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"sandbox-proxy\"}],\" — configuring your org's egress gateway for dev work: which hosts are reachable, how to debug \\\"connection refused\\\" errors, how to add an allowlist entry.\"]}],\"\\n\"]}]\n2f:[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"2-product-verification\",\"children\":\"2. Product verification\"}]\n30:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"These are skills that describe how to test or verify that your code is working. They are often paired with playwright, tmux, or other external tools for verification.\"}]\n31:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Verification skills have had the most measurable impact on Claude’s output quality internally. It can be worth having an engineer spend a week just making your verification skills excellent.\"}]\n32:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Consider techniques like having Claude record a video of its output so you can see exactly what it tested, or enforcing programmatic assertions on state at each step. These are often done by including a variety of scripts in the skill.\"}]\n33:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Examples include:\"}]\n34:[\"$\",\"ul\",null,{\"children\":[\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"signup-flow-driver\"}],\" — runs through signup → email verify → onboarding in a headless browser, with hooks for asserting state at each step\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"checkout-verifier\"}],\" — drives the checkout UI with Stripe test cards, verifies the invoice actually lands in the right state\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"tmux-cli-driver\"}],\" — for interactive CLI testing where the thing you're verifying needs a TTY\"]}],\"\\n\"]}]\n35:[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"3-data-fetching-and-analysis\",\"children\":\"3. Data fetching and analysis\"}]\n36:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"These are skills that connect to your data and monitoring stacks. These skills might include libraries to fetch your data with credentials, specific dashboard ids, etc., as well as instructions on common workflows or ways to get data.\"}]\n37:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Examples include:\"}]\n38:[\"$\",\"ul\",null,{\"children\":[\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"funnel-query\"}],\" — \\\"which events do I join to see signup → activation → paid\\\" plus the table that actually has the canonical user_id\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"cohort-compare\"}],\" — compare two cohorts' retention or conversion, flag statistically significant deltas, link to the segment definitions\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"grafana\"}],\" — datasource UIDs, cluster names, problem → dashboard lookup table\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"datadog\"}],\" — field reference (@request_id vs trace_id), service list, metric prefix conventions\"]}],\"\\n\"]}]\n39:[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"4-business-process-and-team-automation\",\"children\":\"4. Business process and team automation\"}]\n3a:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"These are skills that automate repetitive workflows into one command. These skills are usually fairly simple instructions but might have more complicated dependencies on other skills or MCPs. For these skills, saving previous results in log files can help the model stay consistent and reflect on previous executions of the workflow.\"}]\n3b:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Examples include:\"}]\n3c:[\"$\",\"ul\",null,{\"children\":[\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"standup-post\"}],\" — aggregates your ticket tracker, GitHub activity, and prior Slack → formatted standup, delta-only\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"create-\u003cticket-system\u003e-ticket\"}],\" — enforces schema (valid enum values, required fields) plus post-creation workflow (ping reviewer, link in Slack)\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"weekly-recap\"}],\" — merged PRs + closed tickets + deploys → formatted recap post\"]}],\"\\n\"]}]\n3d:[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"5-code-scaffolding-and-templates\",\"children\":\"5. Code scaffolding and templates\"}]\n3e:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"These are skills that generate framework boilerplates for a specific function in a codebase. You might combine these skills with scripts that can be composed. They are especially useful when your scaffolding has natural language requirements that can’t be purely covered by code.\"}]\n3f:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Examples include:\"}]\n40:[\"$\",\"ul\",null,{\"children\":[\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"new-\u003cframework\u003e-workflow\"}],\" — scaffolds a new service/workflow/handler with your annotations\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"new-migration\"}],\" — your migration file template plus common gotchas\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"create-app\"}],\" — new internal app with your auth, logging, and deploy config pre-wired\"]}],\"\\n\"]}]\n41:[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"6-code-quality-and-review\",\"children\":\"6. Code quality and review\"}]\n42:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"These are skills that enforce code quality inside of your org and help review code. These can include deterministic scripts or tools for maximum robustness. You may want to run these skills automatically as part of hooks or inside of a GitHub Action.\"}]\n43:[\"$\",\"ul\",null,{\"children\":[\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"adversarial-review\"}],\" — spawns a fresh-eyes subagent to critique, implements fixes, iterates until findings degrade to nitpicks\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"code-style\"}],\" — enforces code style, especially styles that Claude does not do well by default.\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"testing-practices\"}],\" — instructions on how to write tests and what to test.\"]}],\"\\n\"]}]\n44:[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"7-cicd-and-deployment\",\"children\":\"7. CI/CD and deployment\"}]\n45:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"These are skills that help you fetch, push, and deploy code inside of your codebase. These skills may reference other skills to collect data.\"}]\n46:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Examples include:\"}]\n47:[\"$\",\"ul\",null,{\"children\":[\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"babysit-pr\"}],\" — monitors a PR → retries flaky CI → resolves merge conflicts → enables auto-merge\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"deploy-\u003cservice\u003e\"}],\" — build → smoke test → gradual traffic rollout with error-rate comparison → auto-rollback on regression\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"cherry-pick-prod\"}],\" — isolated worktree → cherry-pick → conflict resolution → PR with template\"]}],\"\\n\"]}]\n48:[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"8-runbooks\",\"children\":\"8. Runbooks\"}]\n49:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"These are skills that take a symptom (such as a Slack thread, alert, or error signature), walk through a multi-tool investigation, and produce a structured report.\"}]\n4a:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Examples include:\"}]\n4b:[\"$\",\"ul\",null,{\"children\":[\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"\u003cservice\u003e-debugging\"}],\" — maps symptoms → tools → query patterns for your highest-traffic services\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"oncall-runner\"}],\" — fetches the alert → checks the usual suspects → formats a finding\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"log-correlator\"}],\" — given a request ID, pulls matching logs from every system that might have touched it\"]}],\"\\n\"]}]\n4c:[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"9-infrastructure-operations\",\"children\":\"9. Infrastructure operations\"}]\n4d:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"These are skills that perform routine maintenance and operational procedures, some of which involve destructive actions that benefit from guardrails. These make it easier for engineers to follow best practices in critical operations.\"}]\n4e:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Examples include:\"}]\n4f:[\"$\",\"ul\",null,{\"children\":[\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"\u003cresource\u003e-orphans\"}],\" — finds orphaned pods/volumes → posts to Slack → soak period → user confirms → cascading cleanup\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"dependency-management\"}],\" — your org's dependency approval workflow\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"cost-investigation\"}],\" — \\\"why did our storage/egress bill spike\\\" with the specific buckets and query patterns\"]}],\"\\n\"]}]\n50:[\"$\",\"section\",null,{\"className\":\"art-section\",\"data-reveal\":\"\",\"style\":\"$2b:0:props:style\",\"id\":\"lessons-from-building-claude-code-how-we-use-skills-s3\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"h2\",null,{\"id\":\"tips-for-making-skills\",\"children\":[\"TIPS FOR MAKING SKILLS\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Once you've decided on the skill to make, how do you write it? These are some of the Claude Code team’s best practices, tips, and tricks for making skills.\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"dont-state-the-obvious\",\"children\":\"Don’t state the obvious\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Claude already knows how to code and can read your codebase. A skill that restates what Claude would do by default adds context without adding value. If you’re publishing a skill that is primarily about knowledge, focus on information that pushes Claude out of its normal way of thinking.\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":[\"The \",[\"$\",\"a\",null,{\"href\":\"https://github.com/anthropics/skills/blob/main/skills/frontend-design/SKILL.md\",\"children\":\"frontend design skill\"}],\" is a great example; it was built by an engineer at Anthropic by iterating with customers on improving Claude’s design taste, avoiding classic patterns like the Inter font and purple gradients.\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"build-a-gotchas-section\",\"children\":\"Build a gotchas section\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"figure\",null,{\"className\":\"art-fig\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"img\",null,{\"className\":\"fg\",\"src\":\"/media/16acf64a5f80810ad01275e7a7de64b689ff947b145ee1b188f328e614cdfe98.png\",\"alt\":\"The same Billing Lib skill file on day 1, week 2 and month 3. A Gotchas section appears and grows from one line (proration rounds down) to four.\",\"loading\":\"lazy\",\"decoding\":\"async\",\"width\":820,\"height\":360,\"style\":{\"display\":\"block\",\"width\":\"100%\",\"aspectRatio\":\"820 / 360\"}}],null]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"The highest-signal content in any skill is the Gotchas section. These sections should be built up from common failure points that Claude runs into when using your skill. Ideally, you will update your skill over time to capture these gotchas.\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"For example:\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"ul\",null,{\"children\":[\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[\"\\\"The \",[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"subscriptions\"}],\" table is append-only. The row you want is the one with the highest version, not the most recent \",[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"created_at\"}],\".\\\"\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[\"\\\"This field is called \",[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"@request_id\"}],\" in the API gateway and \",[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"trace_id\"}],\" in the billing service. They're the same value.\\\"\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[\"\\\"Staging returns 200 even when the Stripe webhook didn't actually process. Check \",[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"payment_events\"}],\" for the real state.\\\"\"]}],\"\\n\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"use-the-file-system-and-progressive-disclosure\",\"children\":\"Use the file system and progressive disclosure\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"figure\",null,{\"className\":\"art-fig\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"img\",null,{\"className\":\"fg\",\"src\":\"/media/d70d147c4c600c297d350ebd7a76f110c879ca670f9e40adb83b05882f71dd8c.png\",\"alt\":\"A queue-debugging skill folder where SKILL.md is the hub and stuck-jobs.md, dead-letters.md, retry-storms.md and consumer-lag.md are spokes. For example, if a job is pending, it should reference stuck-jobs.md.\"}]]}]]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Like we said earlier, a skill is a folder, not just a markdown file. You should think of the entire file system as a form of context engineering and progressive disclosure. Tell Claude what files are in your skill, and it will read them at appropriate times.\"}],\"\\n\",\"$L56\",\"\\n\",\"$L57\",\"\\n\",\"$L58\",\"\\n\",\"$L59\",\"\\n\",\"$L5a\",\"\\n\",\"$L5b\",\"\\n\",\"$L5c\",\"\\n\",\"$L5d\",\"\\n\",\"$L5e\",\"\\n\",\"$L5f\",\"\\n\",\"$L60\",\"\\n\",\"$L61\",\"\\n\",\"$L62\",\"\\n\",\"$L63\",\"\\n\",\"$L64\",\"\\n\",\"$L65\",\"\\n\",\"$L66\",\"\\n\",\"$L67\",\"\\n\",\"$L68\",\"\\n\",\"$L69\",\"\\n\",\"$L6a\",\"\\n\",\"$L6b\",\"\\n\",\"$L6c\",\"\\n\",\"$L6d\",\"\\n\",\"$L6e\",\"\\n\",\"$L6f\",\"\\n\",\"$L70\",\"\\n\",\"$L71\",\"\\n\",\"$L72\",\"\\n\",\"$L73\",\"\\n\"]}]\n51:[\"$\",\"section\",null,{\"className\":\"art-section\",\"data-reveal\":\"\",\"style\":\"$2b:0:props:style\",\"id\":\"lessons-from-building-claude-code-how-we-use-skills-s4\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"h2\",null,{\"id\":\"distributing-skills\",\"children\":[\"DISTRIBUTING SKILLS\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"One of the biggest benefits of skills is that you can share them with the rest of your team.\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"There are two ways you might want to share skills with others:\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"ul\",null,{\"children\":[\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[\"check your skills into your repo (under \",[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"./.claude/skills\"}],\")\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[\"make a \",[\"$\",\"strong\",null,{\"children\":\"plugin\"}],\" and have a Claude Code Plugin marketplace where users can upload and install plugins (read more on the \",[\"$\",\"a\",null,{\"href\":\"https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-marketplaces\",\"children\":\"documentation\"}],\" here)\"]}],\"\\n\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"For smaller teams working across relatively few repos, checking your skills into repos works well. But every skill that is checked in also adds a little bit to the context of the model. As you scale, an internal plugin marketplace allows you to distribute skills and let your team decide which ones to install, as well as include a setup flow.\"}],\"\\n\"]}]\n52:[\"$\",\"section\",null,{\"className\":\"art-section\",\"data-reveal\":\"\",\"style\":\"$2b:0:props:style\",\"id\":\"lessons-from-building-claude-code-how-we-use-skills-s5\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"h2\",null,{\"id\":\"managing-a-skills-marketplace\",\"children\":[\"MANAGING A SKILLS MARKETPLACE\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"How do you decide which skills go in a marketplace? How do people submit them?\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"At Anthropic, we don't have a centralized team that decides; instead we try to find the most useful skills organically. If someone has a skill that they want people to try out, they can upload it to a sandbox folder in GitHub and point people to it in Slack or other forums.\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Once a skill has gotten traction (which is up to the skill owner to decide), they can put in a PR to move it into the marketplace.\"}],\"\\n\"]}]\n53:[\"$\",\"section\",null,{\"className\":\"art-section\",\"data-reveal\":\"\",\"style\":\"$2b:0:props:style\",\"id\":\"lessons-from-building-claude-code-how-we-use-skills-s6\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"h2\",null,{\"id\":\"composing-skills\",\"children\":[\"COMPOSING SKILLS\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"You may want to have skills that depend on each other. For example, you may have a file upload skill that uploads a file, and a CSV generation skill that makes a CSV and uploads it. This sort of dependency management is not natively built into marketplaces or skills yet, but you can just reference other skills by name, and the model will invoke them if they are installed.\"}],\"\\n\"]}]\n54:[\"$\",\"section\",null,{\"className\":\"art-section\",\"data-reveal\":\"\",\"style\":\"$2b:0:props:style\",\"id\":\"lessons-from-building-claude-code-how-we-use-skills-s7\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"h2\",null,{\"id\":\"measuring-skills\",\"children\":[\"MEASURING SKILLS\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":[\"To understand how a skill is doing, we use a PreToolUse hook that lets us log skill usage within the company (\",[\"$\",\"a\",null,{\"href\":\"https://gist.github.com/ThariqS/24defad423d701746e23dc19aace4de5\",\"children\":\"example code here\"}],\"). This means we can find skills that are popular or are undertriggering compared to our expectations.\"]}],\"\\n\"]}]\n55:[\"$\",\"section\",null,{\"className\":\"art-section\",\"data-reveal\":\"\",\"style\":\"$2b:0:props:style\",\"id\":\"lessons-from-building-claude-code-how-we-use-skills-s8\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"h2\",null,{\"id\":\"get-started\",\"children\":[\"GET STARTED\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Skills best practices are still evolving. Most of our best skills began as a few lines and a single gotcha, then got better because people kept adding to them as Claude hit new edge cases.\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"The best way to understand skills is to get started, experiment, and see what works for you.\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"ul\",null,{\"children\":[\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[\"Check out \",[\"$\",\"a\",null,{\"href\":\"https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills\",\"children\":\"our skills documentation\"}]]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[\"$\",\"a\",null,{\"href\":\"https://github.com/anthropics/skills\",\"children\":\"Find example skills to customize\"}]}],\"\\n\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":[\"$\",\"em\",null,{\"children\":\"This article was written by Thariq Shihipar, a member of technical staff at Anthropic, working on Claude Code.\"}]}]]}]\n56:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":[\"The simplest form of progressive disclosure is to point to other markdown files for Claude to use. For example, you may split detailed function signatures and usage examples into \",[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"references/api.md\"}],\".\"]}]\n57:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":[\"Another example: if your end output is a markdown file, you might include a template file for it in \",[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"assets/\"}],\" to copy and use.\"]}]\n58:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"You can have folders of references, scripts, examples, etc., which help Claude work more effectively.\"}]\n59:[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"avoid-railroading-claude\",\"children\":\"Avoid railroading Claude\"}]\n5a:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Claude will generally try to stick to your instructions, and because skills are so reusable you’ll want to be careful of being too specific in your instructions. Give Claude the information it needs, but give it the flexibility to adapt to the situation.\"}]\n5b:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"For example:\"}]\n5c:[\"$\",\"figure\",null,{\"className\":\"art-fig\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"img\",null,{\"className\":\"fg\",\"src\":\"/media/f634d39724ba5a2785fa6a8aa5614a1e4654c1d278a2d73b0e3b7ce0a74d84c4.png\",\"alt\":\"Two versions of cherry-pick instructions. If it can’t land cleanly, explain why.”\",\"loading\":\"lazy\",\"decoding\":\"async\",\"width\":1440,\"height\":660,\"style\":{\"display\":\"block\",\"width\":\"100%\",\"aspectRatio\":\"1440 / 660\"}}],[\"$\",\"figcaption\",null,{\"className\":\"cap\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"b\",null,{\"children\":\"FIG C\"}],\"$undefined\",[\"$\",\"span\",null,{\"children\":\"State the goal and the constraints, not every step.\"}]]}]]}]\n5d:[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"think-through-the-setup\",\"children\":\"Think through the setup\"}]\n5e:[\"$\",\"figure\",null,{\"className\":\"art-fig\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"img\",null,{\"className\":\"fg\",\"src\":\"/media/c24d1f6d68756396e649a2a1ee89dcde197dad5675e9b75cf17099064345486e.png\",\"alt\":\"A standup-post SKILL.md whose “Your config” section runs a shell command reading config.json and echoing NOT_CONFIGURED if it is missing; the instructions tell Claude to ask for the Slack channel and a sample standup when unconfigured, then save the answers.\",\"loading\":\"lazy\",\"decoding\":\"async\",\"width\":1404,\"height\":818,\"style\":{\"display\":\"block\",\"width\":\"100%\",\"aspectRatio\":\"1404 / 818\"}}],[\"$\",\"figcaption\",null,{\"className\":\"cap\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"b\",null,{\"children\":\"FIG D\"}],\"$undefined\",[\"$\",\"span\",null,{\"children\":\"The skill above is written to prompt the user if the Slack channel is not included in the configuration.\"}]]}]]}]\n5f:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Some skills may need to be set up with context from the user. For example, if you are making a skill that posts your standup to Slack, you may want Claude to ask which Slack channel to post it in.\"}]\n60:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"A good pattern to do this is to store this setup information in a config.json file in the skill directory like the above example. If the config is not set up, the agent can then ask the user for information.\"}]\n61:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"If you want the agent to present structured, multiple choice questions you can instruct Claude to use the AskUserQuestion tool.\"}]\n62:[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"write-descriptions-for-the-model-not-for-humans\",\"children\":\"Write descriptions for the model, not for humans\"}]\n63:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"When Claude Code starts a session, it builds a listing of every available skill with its description. This listing is what Claude scans to decide \\\"is there a skill for this request?\\\" Which means the description field is not a summary, it's a description of when to trigger this skill.\"}]\n64:[\"$\",\"figure\",null,{\"className\":\"art-fig\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"img\",null,{\"className\":\"fg\",\"src\":\"/media/1debbf1fd04f39bcfeb62bcb458574268414bd0f519c4390d708bbac8f1b724e.png\",\"alt\":\"Two SKILL.md descriptions for babysit-pr.
